description: Planning and installation of new single-split and multi-split air conditioning systems in Munich and the Munich district.
h1: Split air conditioning installation in Munich
intro: Split air conditioning can provide targeted comfort cooling without a central duct network, but the apparent simplicity of the system should not obscure the planning involved. The indoor and outdoor units, refrigerant lines, condensate route, power supply and permissions form one installation. This page covers new single-split and multi-split projects in Munich and the Munich district, including installations added to existing buildings.
heroImageAlt: Test gauges used while commissioning a split air conditioning system

sections.title: Single-split or multi-split?
sections.intro: The basic choice is whether one defined area needs an independent system or several rooms need individual indoor units. The answer depends on room use, simultaneous demand, available outdoor space and the routes that can be installed. Neither arrangement is universally better; the building and cooling objectives determine which one is more appropriate.

subsections.title: Single-split for one room
subsections.text: A single-split arrangement pairs one indoor unit with one outdoor unit. It is suited to a clearly defined room or open zone where independent control is required. Planning still needs to account for air distribution, capacity, outdoor-unit placement, the wall penetration and condensate drainage, so the shortest route is not automatically the best overall position.

subsections.title: Multi-split for multiple rooms
subsections.text: Multi-split connects several indoor units to a shared outdoor unit and allows rooms to be controlled separately. It can be useful where several rooms need cooling but outdoor-unit locations are limited. The combined capacity, permitted unit combinations, pipe lengths, simultaneous use and maintenance access all need to be checked as part of one system design.

sections.title: Which system suits your building?
sections.intro: Product type alone cannot answer whether a split system fits a property. Room loads, unit locations, structural routes and drainage determine how the equipment can be integrated. A good concept balances cooling performance with practical installation, access and the effect on occupants and neighbours.

subsections.title: Room use and heat gain
subsections.text: A bedroom used at night has a different load pattern from a glazed living room, an occupied office or a room with heat-producing equipment. Floor area is only one input; orientation, glazing, insulation, occupancy and operating hours also matter. These details help avoid choosing capacity from a simple square-metre rule that ignores how the room actually behaves.

subsections.title: Positioning indoor and outdoor units
subsections.text: The indoor unit should distribute air through the occupied area while remaining accessible for normal user care and future professional access. The outdoor unit needs unobstructed airflow, a stable mounting location and consideration of noise, vibration, appearance and permissions. Both positions must be assessed together because each constrains the connecting route.

subsections.title: Pipe route and condensate drainage
subsections.text: The route normally carries insulated refrigerant lines, control or power connections as specified, and a condensate drain where required. It should be planned to protect drainage fall, avoid unnecessary length and limit disruption to finished surfaces. If gravity drainage is not possible, any alternative must be assessed explicitly rather than assumed after mounting has begun.

sections.imageAlt: Licensed illustrative image for split air conditioning planning

sections.title: What does the installation include?
sections.intro: The installation scope should describe the work required to turn specified equipment into a commissioned system. It must distinguish the core refrigeration and mounting work from electrical, access, making-good or other building work. This prevents the word “installation” from hiding exclusions that are essential to completing the project.

subsections.title: Mounting the units
subsections.text: Mounting includes setting out and securing the indoor and outdoor units on surfaces and supports suitable for the agreed positions. The method depends on the building fabric, vibration control, weather exposure and access. Any facade, roof, balcony or elevated work must be included only after the relevant permissions and safe working method have been established.

subsections.title: Refrigerant lines and leak testing
subsections.text: The refrigerant circuit must be installed using components, joints and procedures appropriate to the selected system. The connected circuit is then checked using the required technical process before commissioning. The responsible qualified party and the exact test and documentation scope must be confirmed for the project rather than inferred from generic marketing language.

subsections.title: Commissioning and user handover
subsections.text: Commissioning verifies that the installed system starts and operates under the conditions available at handover and that relevant settings and drainage can be checked. The user handover should cover basic controls, modes and the documents supplied with the installation. It is not a substitute for the manufacturer’s instructions or for any future service requirements stated for the equipment.

sections.title: Requirements before the installation date
sections.intro: Installation should not be scheduled until the site is ready for the agreed work. Permissions, unit locations, access, electrical responsibility and exclusions need to be settled in advance. A clear preparation stage reduces the risk of discovering on the day that a route, support or connection cannot be used.

subsections.title: Permissions and access
subsections.text: Written landlord or owners’ association approval may be needed depending on ownership and the parts of the building affected. Access must cover the rooms, proposed route, outdoor position and any common areas required to bring in equipment or work safely. Keys, site contacts, building rules and working-hour restrictions should be agreed before the appointment.

subsections.title: Electrical interface
subsections.text: The system’s electrical requirements must be compared with the available supply and the manufacturer’s installation requirements. Where a new circuit, isolator, protection or fixed connection is needed, responsibility for that work must be assigned to an appropriately qualified electrical party. The quote should identify whether this work is included, separately coordinated or excluded.

subsections.title: Agreed scope of work
subsections.text: The agreed scope should identify the equipment, unit locations, principal route, included installation steps, tests, handover documents and any making-good. It should also list exclusions and client responsibilities, such as permissions or access. This written boundary is particularly important where refrigeration, electrical and building work meet.

faq.question: What is the difference between single-split and multi-split?
faq.answer: Single-split uses one indoor unit and one outdoor unit for a defined room or zone. Multi-split connects several indoor units to a shared outdoor unit so that multiple rooms can be controlled separately. Multi-split may reduce the number of outdoor units, but it requires coordinated capacity and more extensive routing. The best option depends on room use, simultaneous demand, available outdoor positions and the permitted combinations of the selected system.

faq.question: How is the right capacity determined?
faq.answer: Capacity should be based on the cooling demand of the specific room, not floor area alone. Relevant inputs include size, orientation, glazing, insulation, ceiling height, occupancy, equipment and operating hours. The proposed indoor-unit position and airflow also matter. A technical assessment combines these factors with the performance characteristics of the system being considered.

faq.question: Where can the outdoor unit be installed?
faq.answer: Possible locations can include a suitable balcony area, facade position, terrace, roof or ground-level base, but none is automatically acceptable. The location must provide airflow, stable support, drainage where relevant, safe access and consideration of noise, vibration, weather and external appearance. Ownership, landlord or owners’ association approval and any building-specific restrictions must be clarified before the position is confirmed.

faq.question: How is condensate drained?
faq.answer: Condensate from the indoor unit is normally directed to an approved drainage point using a route with reliable fall. The outlet must not create water damage, staining, icing or nuisance to neighbours or public areas. Where gravity drainage cannot be achieved, an alternative such as a suitable pump may need assessment, but its noise, access and failure implications should be considered before it is selected.

faq.question: May I connect the system myself?
faq.answer: The equipment may be purchased by a customer, but work on the refrigerant circuit and commissioning is not a DIY connection task. It must be carried out by appropriately qualified and, where applicable, certified persons or businesses under the rules applying to the system and refrigerant. Fixed electrical work also belongs with the relevant qualified trade. Buying equipment first can create compatibility and documentation problems, so the complete scope should be checked beforehand.

title: Apartment air conditioning installation Munich | IsarKlima
description: Split air conditioning for rental or owner-occupied apartments: permissions, planning and installation in Munich.
h1: Apartment air conditioning installation in Munich
intro: Installing split air conditioning in an apartment requires technical planning and a clear understanding of who can approve changes to the building. The indoor unit may be inside the private dwelling, while the outdoor unit, facade, balcony or wall penetration can affect rented property or common ownership. The process should therefore begin with permission and a realistic installation route, not with ordering equipment.
heroImageAlt: Bright apartment living space illustrating indoor comfort

sections.title: Rental or owner-occupied apartment: clarify permission first
sections.intro: The route to approval differs between a rented apartment and a condominium, but in both cases written clarity is preferable before technical work is booked. An outdoor unit or penetration can change the building fabric or appearance even if the indoor equipment is entirely within the apartment. The proposed position, route, noise treatment and condensate solution help the decision-maker understand what is being requested.

subsections.title: Landlord’s consent
subsections.text: A tenant should present the landlord with a concrete proposal rather than a general request for “air conditioning”. Useful information includes the unit positions, wall penetration, external appearance, pipe route, condensate discharge and how the installation would be fixed. Written consent should be obtained before installation; any conditions concerning restoration, contractors or documentation must be reflected in the project scope.

subsections.title: Owners’ association resolution
subsections.text: In a condominium, work may affect common property or the building’s external appearance even when it serves one apartment. The proposed facade, balcony or wall work should be submitted through the appropriate owners’ association process, with property management involved where applicable. Whether a formal resolution is needed depends on the measure and property context, so the approval position should be clarified before a date is agreed.

sections.title: The right split system for your apartment
sections.intro: Apartment layouts often make room-by-room priorities more useful than an attempt to cool every space indirectly. The choice between single-split and multi-split should consider closed doors, room use, outdoor-unit options and the routes available through finished areas. Cooling one key room well can be more realistic than expecting one indoor unit to control an entire apartment.

subsections.title: Cooling one room
subsections.text: A single-split system can target the room with the highest or most important cooling demand, such as a bedroom or main living area. The indoor position should support air circulation without directing a continuous draught at beds or seating. The feasibility of the outdoor position and a discreet, drainable route remains just as important as the room itself.

subsections.title: Controlling several rooms separately
subsections.text: Several indoor units allow bedrooms, living areas or workspaces to be controlled individually, which can suit rooms used at different times. A multi-split system may connect them to one outdoor unit, subject to system limits and route feasibility. Each room still needs its own capacity and airflow assessment; an equal unit in every room is not automatically an appropriate design.

sections.imageAlt: Licensed illustrative image for split air conditioning planning

sections.title: Positioning the outdoor unit responsibly
sections.intro: The outdoor unit is usually the most sensitive part of an apartment project because it can be visible, audible and located on or near common property. A position should be assessed for airflow, access, support, vibration transfer and its effect on neighbours. Permission and technical suitability must point to the same location before it is accepted.

subsections.title: Facade, balcony or suitable installation area
subsections.text: A facade position may offer a direct route but can affect appearance, common property and working-at-height requirements. A balcony can provide access, yet still needs sufficient airflow, stable support and compliance with ownership rules. Any other installation area must be evaluated for the same technical and permission constraints rather than chosen only because it is out of sight.

subsections.title: Noise and vibration
subsections.text: Outdoor-unit sound can be amplified by hard surfaces, corners or lightweight structures, while vibration can travel through brackets and building elements. Position, mounting system and separation from sensitive windows or neighbouring spaces should be considered together. Published equipment data is useful, but it does not by itself predict the sound experienced at a particular property boundary or room.

subsections.title: Safe condensate drainage
subsections.text: Condensate must be routed to a suitable point without dripping over the facade, onto another property or across a walking surface. The drainage route needs adequate fall, protection and access for the arrangement selected. Where a pump is considered, its location, sound and accessibility should be assessed as part of the installation rather than added as an afterthought.

sections.title: Apartment installation process
sections.intro: The process is designed to resolve ownership and building constraints before surfaces are drilled or equipment is mounted. Documents and photographs support an initial review, followed by route agreement and an on-site check where necessary. Installation proceeds only against a defined scope and approved positions.

subsections.title: Reviewing documents and photos
subsections.text: Useful material includes a simple plan, room dimensions, photographs of the rooms and balcony or facade, and any landlord or owners’ association conditions already received. Images should show the wider context as well as close details, because access and neighbouring windows can matter. This review helps identify missing information; it does not replace an on-site check where measurements or building fabric remain uncertain.

subsections.title: Agreeing the installation route
subsections.text: The route should show where the wall penetration, insulated lines, drainage and covers will run and how they reach the outdoor unit. It must work technically while limiting disruption to finishes and common areas. Any visible trunking, balcony route or facade element should be included in the material presented for permission so that the approved and installed versions do not diverge.

subsections.title: Installation and handover
subsections.text: Installation follows the approved positions and written scope, including the assigned refrigeration, electrical and building tasks. Required checks and commissioning are completed before the basic controls and supplied documents are handed over. If site conditions differ materially from the agreed information, the change should be assessed and approved rather than improvised during the work.

faq.question: Do I need my landlord’s permission?
faq.answer: You should obtain written landlord consent when installation affects the building fabric, exterior or any part you are not authorised to alter independently. A useful request explains the indoor and outdoor positions, wall penetration, pipe route, condensate handling, mounting and visible finish. The landlord may impose conditions, and those conditions must be understood before installation is ordered or scheduled.

faq.question: Does the owners’ association need to approve?
faq.answer: Approval may be required if the outdoor unit, facade work, wall penetration, balcony arrangement or other elements affect common property or the building’s appearance. The exact process depends on the property and proposed measure. Provide sufficiently specific technical information to the property management or owners’ association and obtain the required decision before treating the installation route as available.

faq.question: Can the outdoor unit be placed on the balcony?
faq.answer: A balcony can be possible, but it is not automatically suitable or permitted. The unit needs airflow, stable support, acceptable sound and vibration behaviour, safe drainage and access. Its position must also comply with the landlord or owners’ association decision and must not obstruct escape, use of the balcony or other building requirements. The complete context has to be reviewed.

faq.question: How can noise and vibration be reduced?
faq.answer: Reduction starts with selecting a position away from acoustically sensitive rooms and avoiding corners or surfaces that can amplify sound. Suitable supports and vibration isolation can limit structure-borne transmission when correctly chosen for the unit and substrate. Airflow must remain unobstructed, and sound data should be considered alongside the actual distances, reflections and expected operating periods at the building.

faq.question: What documents should I prepare before enquiring?
faq.answer: Prepare the full address, a floor plan if available, approximate room sizes, photographs of indoor and outdoor areas and a note explaining which rooms need cooling. Add your tenancy or ownership status and any written landlord, property management or owners’ association information. If a specific installation position has already been discussed, include that context without assuming it is technically approved.

formIntro: Describe the apartment, rooms, ownership status and proposed outdoor location, and state whether permission has been requested or received. The project form can collect an initial description once it is activated; a secure method for any supporting documents must be confirmed as part of the final form configuration. Submission is an assessment request, not an order.

title: Home air conditioning installation Munich | IsarKlima
description: New single-split or multi-split air conditioning for homes in Munich, planned around rooms, routes and outdoor location.
h1: Home air conditioning installation in Munich
intro: A house offers more options for indoor and outdoor unit placement than many apartments, but it also presents a wider range of room loads and possible routes. A bedroom under the roof, a glazed living area and a ground-floor home office do not need the same solution. New and retrofit split installations should therefore be planned around the rooms that actually require cooling, the construction of the house and the practical path for each connection.
heroImageAlt: Wall-mounted split air conditioning unit in a home interior

sections.title: Cooling one room or several living areas
sections.intro: The first decision is whether cooling is needed in one priority area or across several zones that are used independently. Open doors and staircases do not guarantee useful cooling in remote rooms, so the expected result should be defined room by room. Single-split and multi-split systems provide different ways to meet that need without assuming that every part of the house must be treated alike.

subsections.title: Single-split for one specific area
subsections.text: A single-split system can serve a bedroom, living room, attic room or home office with its own indoor and outdoor unit. It is most effective when the intended cooling area is clearly defined and air can circulate within that space. The indoor position, outdoor location, pipe route and condensate solution must still be planned as a complete installation.

subsections.title: Multi-split for multiple zones
subsections.text: Multi-split can connect indoor units in several rooms to one outdoor unit, allowing each zone to be controlled separately. It may be useful where outdoor space or visual impact limits the number of external units. The design needs to account for the capacity assigned to each room, simultaneous operation, pipe lengths and the locations available for routing through the house.

sections.title: Matching capacity and unit positions to your needs
sections.intro: Capacity and placement should be developed together. A correctly sized unit in a poor position can create uneven temperatures or intrusive airflow, while a convenient outdoor location can impose an impractical route. The assessment considers how the rooms gain heat, how occupants use them and how the equipment can be integrated without compromising access or neighbouring properties.

subsections.title: Room size, use and solar gain
subsections.text: Floor area is only the starting point. Glazing, orientation, insulation, ceiling height, roof exposure, occupancy and electrical equipment can materially change the cooling demand. Operating patterns also matter: a bedroom used overnight differs from a sunlit living room used throughout the day. These inputs support a capacity assessment specific to each proposed indoor unit.

subsections.title: Air distribution in the room
subsections.text: The indoor unit should send conditioned air through the occupied area without blowing continuously at beds, desks or seating. Walls, furniture, beams and door positions can interrupt circulation, and cooling should not be expected to travel reliably around closed corners into other rooms. Placement is therefore chosen for the actual layout, not simply for the shortest external route.

subsections.title: Outdoor location and neighbours
subsections.text: The outdoor unit needs free airflow, stable support, weather-suitable positioning and access for the installation. It should also be assessed in relation to neighbouring windows, terraces, property boundaries and sound-sensitive spaces. A visually hidden position is not necessarily acoustically or technically suitable, particularly if walls or corners reflect sound or restrict discharge air.

sections.imageAlt: Licensed illustrative image for split air conditioning planning

sections.title: Preparing installation in an existing or new building
sections.intro: Existing houses require routes that respect finished surfaces and unknown construction details, while new builds offer the chance to coordinate openings, services and finishes earlier. In both cases, unit positions and responsibilities should be confirmed before work reaches a stage where changes become disruptive. Early planning is valuable even though the split equipment itself may be selected later.

subsections.title: Planning pipe routes early
subsections.text: An early route plan can reserve wall penetrations, sleeves, service zones and suitable paths for insulated lines and drainage. In an existing house, it helps compare visible trunking with more involved concealed work before either is assumed. In a new build, the route should be coordinated with structure, airtightness, insulation and interior finishes rather than added independently.

subsections.title: Power supply and condensate
subsections.text: The electrical requirements of the proposed system must be matched to the planned or existing supply, with any fixed work assigned to the qualified electrical party. Condensate needs a safe destination and a route with suitable fall or an assessed alternative. Both interfaces should be planned before walls and ceilings are closed or unit positions are treated as final.

sections.title: How the system is installed
sections.intro: The installation sequence follows a technical pre-check, a written scope and confirmed access. Mounting, connection, checking and handover are related stages, but other trades or preparatory work may be required between them. The project description should make these boundaries visible before an installation date is set.

subsections.title: Technical pre-check
subsections.text: The pre-check reviews room loads, unit positions, route dimensions, mounting surfaces, drainage, power and outdoor access. It also identifies permissions or specialist work that must be completed first. Clear photographs and plans can support this stage, but site measurements are needed where the building or route cannot be confirmed remotely.

subsections.title: Mounting and connection
subsections.text: The units and specified supports are mounted in the agreed positions, and the refrigerant, condensate and control connections are installed along the defined route. Electrical and building interfaces are completed by the responsible qualified parties according to the agreed division of work. Any material change in route or position should be reviewed before it is executed.

subsections.title: Testing and user handover
subsections.text: The connected system undergoes the checks and commissioning steps applicable to the installed equipment and scope. The handover covers basic controls, relevant operating information and the documents supplied for the project. It should also make clear which future care belongs to the user and which activities require appropriately qualified professional work.

faq.question: Is one indoor unit enough for the whole house?
faq.answer: Usually, one indoor unit should be understood as cooling the room or open zone in which it is installed. Air does not move predictably through closed doors, around stairs or into separate bedrooms, and temperature differences can remain significant. An assessment should identify the priority rooms and realistic airflow rather than promise whole-house cooling from a single point.

faq.question: When does multi-split make sense?
faq.answer: Multi-split can make sense when several separate rooms need individual control and a shared outdoor unit is preferable or necessary. It is particularly relevant when outdoor positions are limited, but the permitted unit combinations, total demand, pipe routes and simultaneous operation must work for the selected system. Separate single-split systems may be more appropriate in other layouts, so the decision is project-specific.

faq.question: Where should the outdoor unit be placed?
faq.answer: The preferred location combines unobstructed airflow, stable mounting, practical pipe routing, safe access and consideration for neighbours. Ground, wall, terrace and roof positions each create different structural, acoustic and access questions. The final choice should be based on the property, permissions and technical data, not solely on keeping the unit out of view.

faq.question: Can air conditioning be installed in an older building?
faq.answer: An older building can be suitable for a retrofit, but construction, protected elements, wall materials, electrical capacity and feasible routes need checking. Finished surfaces and hidden services can make the installation more involved than in a prepared new build. Feasibility should be established from the actual house, and any conservation or ownership restrictions must be resolved separately where relevant.

faq.question: What should be planned early in a new build?
faq.answer: Identify the rooms to be cooled, likely indoor and outdoor positions, pipe routes, wall or roof penetrations, condensate drainage, electrical provisions and access. These items should be coordinated with structure, insulation, airtightness, facade design and interior finishes. Early provision preserves options; it does not remove the need to select and assess the final system before installation.

Note whether the building is existing, under renovation or in construction and identify any known access or electrical constraints. title: Office air conditioning installation Munich | IsarKlima
description: Split air conditioning for offices and small commercial spaces in Munich, from project planning to handover.
h1: Office and commercial air conditioning installation in Munich
intro: Comfort cooling for an office or smaller commercial unit must reflect the way the space is occupied and operated. People, computers, lighting, glazed areas and opening hours can create loads that are not apparent from floor area alone. The service scope is limited to new and retrofit split systems for offices and small, non-critical commercial spaces; it excludes industrial refrigeration and environments that require specialist or redundant cooling.
heroImageAlt: Technicians installing air conditioning as an illustrative stock image

sections.title: Cooling for offices and small commercial spaces
sections.intro: Some projects involve one enclosed room with a clear heat problem, while others contain several work or customer zones with different schedules. The installation concept should identify those zones and the effect of doors, partitions and internal gains. It should not assume that one unit at the entrance can serve a divided workplace evenly.

subsections.title: Cooling individual rooms
subsections.text: A single-split system can provide independent cooling for a meeting room, office, ordinary workspace or another defined non-critical area. The assessment looks at occupancy, equipment, solar exposure and the times at which the room is used. Unit position should support comfortable distribution without directing persistent airflow at workstations or customer seating.

subsections.title: Serving multiple usage zones
subsections.text: Where several rooms or zones need separate control, a multi-split arrangement or another combination of split systems can be assessed. The design must consider simultaneous demand, different schedules, available outdoor positions and the routes through occupied premises. Each zone retains its own load and airflow requirements even when the outdoor equipment is shared.

sections.title: Adapting the system to use and operating hours
sections.intro: Commercial comfort depends on when heat is generated and when people are present. A space may have a moderate morning load and a much higher afternoon load, or one room may be occupied only for short periods. The technical assessment should capture this pattern so that capacity, control and placement reflect the business use rather than a residential assumption.

subsections.title: People, equipment and internal heat loads
subsections.text: Occupants, computers, displays, lighting and other equipment release heat into the room. Their number, power and operating schedule can materially affect cooling demand, especially in compact or well-glazed spaces. Providing this information helps distinguish a normal comfort-cooling project from a space whose equipment or process would require specialist design outside the stated scope.

subsections.title: Noise-conscious positioning
subsections.text: Indoor units should be placed with attention to workstations, meeting areas and customer-facing zones, while outdoor units must be considered in relation to neighbours and building users. Sound levels depend on operating mode, distance and the acoustic environment, not only a value in a product table. Vibration isolation, airflow and access must remain part of the same positioning decision.

subsections.title: Installation times and access
subsections.text: Work in occupied premises may need coordination with opening hours, deliveries, security, building management and access to common areas. An out-of-hours period can be considered only if the site, building rules, noise constraints and responsible parties allow it. No particular schedule should be promised before the scope and address have been assessed.

sections.imageAlt: Licensed illustrative image for split air conditioning planning

sections.title: From project enquiry to commissioning
sections.intro: The project moves from a description of the rooms and operating needs to an agreed installation plan. The initial review identifies missing load, access and permission information; a site visit can then confirm conditions where needed. Commissioning and handover follow only after the included work and technical interfaces have been defined.

subsections.title: Capturing rooms and requirements
subsections.text: The enquiry should list the rooms, dimensions, occupancy, operating hours, heat-producing equipment and any areas where noise or airflow is particularly sensitive. Plans and photographs help show partitions, windows and possible routes. The project should also state whether the premises are leased and who can approve external or common-area work.

subsections.title: Coordinating the installation scope
subsections.text: Coordination covers unit positions, refrigerant and condensate routes, the electrical interface, access, permissions and any making-good. If a landlord, property manager, electrician or building contractor is involved, each responsibility should be assigned before work begins. The final quote should distinguish the split installation from separately supplied work.

subsections.title: Installation and documented handover
subsections.text: The agreed equipment is mounted and connected, followed by the applicable checks and commissioning. Handover documentation should identify the installed system, basic operating information and the work completed within the agreed scope. Any business-specific records or site procedures required for access or acceptance need to be identified during planning rather than invented after completion.

faq.question: Which commercial spaces can be assessed?
faq.answer: The intended scope covers offices and smaller commercial spaces where split air conditioning is used for normal occupant comfort. Each address and use must still be reviewed. Industrial refrigeration, hotels, hospitals, server or critical rooms and environments requiring specialist process cooling, redundancy or continuous cooling are outside the stated service focus.

faq.question: Can installation take place outside operating hours?
faq.answer: It may be possible to plan work outside normal operating hours, but this depends on the address, building access, management rules, permitted noise, the work involved and the availability actually confirmed for the project. Requirements should be stated in the enquiry. A preferred time is a planning input, not a guaranteed installation slot.

faq.question: How are internal heat loads considered?
faq.answer: The assessment records expected occupancy, computers, lighting, appliances and any other equipment that releases heat during normal use. It also considers glazing, solar gain and operating hours. This information informs the room cooling demand and helps identify cases that fall outside ordinary comfort cooling and require a different specialist scope.

faq.question: Who coordinates any electrical work required?
faq.answer: Responsibility must be stated in the project scope. The split-system assessment identifies the electrical interface specified for the proposed equipment, while any new fixed circuit, protection or connection must be completed by the appropriately qualified electrical party. Until the operating model and any partner arrangements are verified, the website should not claim that a particular electrical service is included.

faq.question: What information is needed for a quote?
faq.answer: Provide the full address, business use, room plan or dimensions, occupancy, operating hours, major heat-producing equipment and desired cooling zones. Add photographs of potential indoor and outdoor positions, access constraints and any landlord or management conditions. State whether out-of-hours work is preferred and whether an electrical assessment already exists. Further technical checks may still be needed before the scope is reliable.

formIntro: Describe the premises, usage zones, occupancy, operating pattern and project address, and identify the person able to approve building work. Include known access, noise and electrical constraints. The enquiry form will not accept live project requests until the dedicated endpoint, privacy details, business authorisation and responsibility for any partner work have been confirmed.

title: Retrofit air conditioning in Munich | IsarKlima
description: Assessing and installing retrofit split air conditioning in existing apartments, homes and offices in Munich.
h1: Retrofit air conditioning in Munich
intro: Retrofitting split air conditioning means finding a practical route through a building that was not necessarily prepared for it. The project must accommodate indoor and outdoor units, insulated lines, condensate drainage, power and access while respecting ownership and finished surfaces. Feasibility depends on the specific address and proposed rooms; it should not be inferred from the building type alone.
heroImageAlt: Outdoor split air conditioning unit installed at a building

sections.title: Can air conditioning be retrofitted in your building?
sections.intro: Many existing buildings can be assessed for a split installation, but not every desired arrangement is feasible or permitted. The essential questions are whether suitable unit locations and a compliant route exist and whether the relevant owner or building body approves the work. A revised layout may be needed if the first idea conflicts with structure, appearance, noise or access.

subsections.title: Space for indoor and outdoor units
subsections.text: Indoor units need wall or ceiling space, airflow and access without obstructing normal use. Outdoor units need ventilation, structural support, weather-suitable positioning and room for installation access. Both locations must be considered together; available space inside does not establish feasibility if there is no acceptable external position.

subsections.title: Pipe route and wall penetration
subsections.text: The route must accommodate insulated refrigerant lines, drainage and associated connections between the units. A wall penetration is commonly part of a split retrofit, but its position and method depend on the construction and route selected. Hidden services, facade systems, fire separations or protected elements may require further investigation or a different approach.

subsections.title: Ownership, consent and building protection
subsections.text: Tenancy, condominium ownership and common property can restrict where equipment and penetrations are permitted. Written consent should identify the proposed external unit and visible route. The installation method must also respect the building fabric, weather protection and any property-specific requirements; approval from an owner is not by itself a technical assessment.

sections.title: Retrofitting apartments, houses and offices
sections.intro: The basic split-system principles are shared across property types, but access, permissions and room use change the practical design. An apartment often places greater emphasis on common property, a house may offer more route options, and an office introduces occupancy and scheduling constraints. Each retrofit is assessed within its real context.

subsections.title: Existing apartment
subsections.text: An apartment retrofit begins with landlord or owners’ association requirements and a viable outdoor position. The route may need to pass through finished rooms or use visible covers, so its appearance should be included in the approval information. Noise, vibration and drainage need particular attention where neighbours and common areas are close.

subsections.title: House and attic floor
subsections.text: Houses and attic rooms can present strong solar loads and longer routes to a suitable outdoor location. Roof construction, insulation, facade details and access at height may affect the installation method. The assessment should compare the cooling need with route complexity rather than assume that the uppermost room is automatically the easiest to connect.

subsections.title: Office and small commercial space
subsections.text: An office retrofit must account for occupants, equipment, opening hours and disruption to the premises. The route, unit positions and work period should be coordinated with the landlord or building management where relevant. Only normal comfort-cooling projects for smaller, non-critical spaces fall within the intended scope.

sections.imageAlt: Licensed illustrative image for split air conditioning planning

sections.title: How installation is prepared
sections.intro: Preparation turns photographs and initial preferences into an agreed scope. It identifies what can be established remotely and what must be measured or inspected at the property. The result should define the proposed system arrangement and the work boundaries before surfaces are opened.

subsections.title: Reviewing photos and project details
subsections.text: Photographs should show whole rooms, possible indoor positions, the external area, likely route and any access constraints. A plan, room measurements and a description of occupancy or use add context. This material can reveal obvious issues and guide questions, but it cannot confirm hidden construction or exact dimensions that require a site check.

subsections.title: Defining the scope clearly
subsections.text: The scope should record the rooms, unit arrangement, locations, route, drainage, electrical interface, permissions, access and making-good. It should list the work included and the tasks assigned to the customer or another trade. Clear exclusions are essential in a retrofit because concealed conditions can otherwise be mistaken for work already priced.

sections.title: What affects installation complexity?
sections.intro: Retrofit complexity is driven less by the age label of a building than by the route and interfaces actually encountered. Working height, surface finishes, distance and preparatory work can change the method substantially. These factors should be described individually rather than reduced to an unsupported standard installation category.

subsections.title: Access and working height
subsections.text: Outdoor units on upper facades, roofs or restricted courtyards may require special access planning or equipment. Indoor work can also be constrained by occupied rooms, narrow stairs or protected common areas. The required access method must be assessed and included before the project is treated as ready for installation.

subsections.title: Pipe route and finishes
subsections.text: A route over accessible, unfinished surfaces differs from one crossing completed interiors, bespoke joinery or a facade system. Decisions about visible trunking, concealed work and reinstatement affect both scope and disruption. The quote should state the intended finish and whether painting, plastering or other making-good is included or separate.

subsections.title: Additional technical work
subsections.text: Electrical modifications, drainage solutions, structural supports, core drilling, access equipment or building repairs may be necessary in addition to the core split installation. Which items apply can be known only after the proposed arrangement is reviewed. Each additional interface should have an identified responsible party and should not be implied as included by a broad headline.

faq.question: Can almost any building be retrofitted?
faq.answer: Many buildings can be considered, but it would be misleading to promise that almost any requested arrangement will work. A project needs acceptable indoor and outdoor locations, a feasible route, drainage, power, access and the required permissions. Construction, protected elements, ownership rules or noise constraints may require a different layout or make the proposed project unsuitable.

faq.question: Is a wall penetration required?
faq.answer: A split system normally needs a route between the indoor and outdoor units, and this commonly includes at least one penetration through the building envelope or another wall. The exact route depends on the property and unit positions. Penetrations must be planned around structure, hidden services, insulation, weather sealing and permission rather than drilled solely at the most direct point.

faq.question: What applies to rental and owner-occupied apartments?
faq.answer: Tenants should obtain written landlord consent for alterations and external equipment. Condominium owners may need approval through the owners’ association where common property or appearance is affected. The proposed unit positions, route, drainage and noise treatment should be described before approval is sought. Property permission and technical feasibility are separate checks, and both are required.

faq.question: How is a discreet pipe route planned?
faq.answer: The route is compared against room layout, drainage fall, permitted lengths, wall construction and the finishes that would be affected. Visible covers can sometimes provide a controlled result with less disruption, while concealed routing may require additional building work and access. “Discreet” should mean an agreed, maintainable solution, not a route hidden at the expense of technical suitability.

faq.question: Which photos help with the initial assessment?
faq.answer: Provide wide images of each room, close and wide views of proposed indoor positions, the complete outdoor area and the likely path between them. Include balconies, facade sections, nearby windows, drainage points, electrical areas and access routes where relevant. A simple annotated plan or sketch can explain how the photographs relate to one another. Avoid sending personal or sensitive documents through an unconfirmed channel.

formIntro: Submit the address, building type, rooms, ownership status and photographs of possible routes and unit positions. Describe which surfaces are finished and whether approval has already been discussed. The form is a future assessment channel and remains inactive until Formspree, privacy, operating qualifications and the scope of accepting real work have been verified.

title: Air conditioning installation costs Munich | IsarKlima
description: Factors that shape the cost of installed split air conditioning in Munich and what a transparent quote should cover.
h1: How much does air conditioning installation cost in Munich?
intro: There is no responsible project price without knowing the rooms, system arrangement and installation route. Equipment is only one part of the scope: mounting, pipework, drainage, electrical interfaces, access and making-good can differ substantially between properties. This page explains what changes the installation cost and what information a quote should contain, without publishing unsupported package prices.
heroImageAlt: Technical gauges used to check an air conditioning system

sections.title: Why the price depends on the project
sections.intro: A quote reflects the complete path from the cooling requirement to a commissioned split system. Similar room sizes do not guarantee similar costs if one project has a direct ground-floor route and another involves several rooms, finished surfaces or restricted access. The cost discussion should therefore begin with scope and assumptions rather than a headline figure.

subsections.title: System type and number of rooms
subsections.text: A single-split installation serves one defined room with one indoor and one outdoor unit. Multi-split serves several rooms through multiple indoor units and a shared outdoor unit, adding capacity coordination and additional routes. Equipment selection and the number of connections both affect the scope, but the lower number of outdoor units does not make multi-split automatically cheaper or simpler.

subsections.title: Pipe length, access and wall penetration
subsections.text: Longer or more complex routes require additional materials, supports, covers and installation time. Wall construction, the number and type of penetrations, working height and access to the outdoor position can change the method. A route that crosses completed interiors or common areas may also require protection and making-good that should be visible in the quote.

subsections.title: Electrical work and other interfaces
subsections.text: The proposed system may require verification of the available supply and, depending on the property and equipment, separate fixed electrical work. Drainage adaptations, structural supports, core drilling, access equipment or finishing work can also sit alongside the core refrigeration installation. The responsible party and commercial treatment of each interface must be stated rather than assumed.

sections.title: What a transparent quote should include
sections.intro: A useful quote allows the customer to compare the technical scope, not just the total. It should identify the equipment or specification basis, the work included and the conditions on which the price relies. Exclusions are as important as inclusions because they show which tasks or risks remain outside the quoted installation.

subsections.title: Equipment and technical specification
subsections.text: The quote should identify the proposed indoor and outdoor arrangement and provide enough specification to understand capacity, system type and the basis of selection. It should not rely on an unexplained model name. Any assumptions about room data, simultaneous operation or customer-supplied equipment should be written down so they can be checked before acceptance.

subsections.title: Included installation work
subsections.text: Included work should describe mounting, the allowed route or pipe length basis, refrigerant connections, condensate handling, specified electrical interface, checks, commissioning and handover where applicable. Supports, covers, penetrations, access measures and making-good should be listed if included. Clear wording reduces disputes over what “standard installation” was intended to cover.

subsections.title: Excluded additional work
subsections.text: Exclusions may include fixed electrical alterations, scaffolding or special access, structural assessment, permits, extensive concealed routing, decoration or repairs to unexpected building conditions. The actual list must be tailored to the project. An exclusion should not hide work that is known to be essential; it should identify who must arrange it and when it must be completed.

sections.title: How to obtain a reliable quote
sections.intro: The quality of the quote depends on the quality of the project information. An address, room data and photographs can support an initial scope, while uncertain routes or building conditions may require a visit. Permissions and timing also affect whether the proposed arrangement can be offered as described.

subsections.title: Address, rooms and use
subsections.text: Provide the exact address, property type, rooms to be cooled, approximate dimensions and how each room is used. Include occupancy, glazing or equipment where they materially affect heat gain. The address is needed to check the service area and building context; it should be handled under the final privacy process once live enquiries are activated.

subsections.title: Photos and possible unit positions
subsections.text: Photographs should show entire rooms, preferred indoor positions, the outdoor area and the likely route between them. Include walls, balconies, facade sections, nearby windows, drainage options and access where relevant. Photos improve the initial assessment, but they do not prove dimensions, wall construction or hidden services that may need checking on site.

subsections.title: Permissions and preferred timing
subsections.text: State whether you are the owner or tenant and whether landlord or owners’ association approval has been obtained, requested or not yet considered. Add the period in which the project is being planned, but do not treat it as confirmed availability. Building access rules and any required coordination with other work should also be disclosed before a quote is finalised.

faq.question: Why do we not quote a flat price?
faq.answer: A flat price would have to assume a system, room load, route length, wall type, outdoor location, drainage, electrical condition and access before any of them were known. Those assumptions could make the figure irrelevant or conceal necessary work. A project quote is based on the actual installation concept and shows what is included, excluded and still subject to verification.

faq.question: Is multi-split always more expensive than single-split?
faq.answer: No universal comparison is possible. Multi-split uses several indoor units with one outdoor unit and can reduce external equipment, but it adds coordinated capacity and multiple routes. Several independent single-split systems use more outdoor units but may offer simpler routes or operating independence in a particular building. Equipment, room count, routing and access must be compared for the actual project.

faq.question: What additional work may be required?
faq.answer: Depending on the property, additional work can include fixed electrical alterations, a condensate solution, specialist drilling, structural supports, access equipment, protection of common areas, concealed routing or making-good. Permissions or separate technical assessments may also be needed. The quote should identify known additional work and state how genuinely unforeseen conditions would be handled before any change is authorised.

faq.question: Is a site visit needed for the quote?
faq.answer: Clear plans, measurements and photographs may support an initial quote or establish that a visit is the next step. A site visit is more likely when the outdoor position, route, wall construction, drainage, power or access cannot be verified remotely. If a visit is required, its purpose and status should be explained; it does not itself create an obligation to proceed.

faq.question: Which items should be listed separately in a quote?
faq.answer: At minimum, the equipment or specification, core installation, route assumptions, supports, penetrations, condensate handling, electrical responsibility, testing and handover should be understandable. Access equipment, extensive building work, decoration and other separately supplied tasks should be identified where relevant. The exact breakdown can vary, but it should allow the customer to see what changes if the scope changes.

subsections.text: Single-split serves one defined room with one indoor and one outdoor unit. Multi-split connects several indoor units to a shared outdoor unit for separate room control. subsections.text: The intended projects are normal comfort-cooling installations in apartments, houses, offices and smaller non-critical commercial premises. subsections.title: Clear project information
subsections.text: Useful information includes the precise address, building and ownership type, room dimensions, use, occupancy and any relevant heat-producing equipment. Photographs and plans should show possible unit locations, access and the connecting route. A clear project record allows missing permissions or interfaces to be identified before equipment or dates are discussed.

subsections.title: Agreed scope of work
subsections.text: The scope should identify the system arrangement, unit positions, route, drainage, electrical interface, access, tests and handover documents. It should distinguish included work from customer responsibilities and separately coordinated trades. Any change prompted by actual site conditions should be reviewed and agreed rather than absorbed informally.

subsections.title: Documented handover
subsections.text: The intended handover records the installed arrangement and the work completed within the agreed scope, alongside the relevant equipment information. It should explain basic operation and identify any documents or responsibilities that remain with the customer. The exact documentation must match the verified operating model and applicable project requirements; it should not be promised in vague or inflated terms.
